items.title: The AI agent blueprint
items.caption:
A useful AI agent starts with a clear task and a way to check the result.

This map separates six pieces that are often bundled together: skills, knowledge sources, subagents, the agent loop, MCP connections and plugins. They solve different problems. Installing more of them does not automatically make an agent more reliable.

Start with the smallest working system. Add retrieval when evidence is missing, delegation when a bounded task benefits from it, and integrations when the task requires an external action. Keep permissions and verification explicit.

Save the map. Which part of your current agent causes the most friction?

items.title: NLP: a developer’s field notebook
items.caption:
You can learn NLP as a connected system instead of a list of acronyms.

I put together a 20-page field notebook that moves from text preprocessing and representations to transformers, retrieval, RAG, evaluation and deployment. Each page explains the decision behind the technique and a common mistake to avoid.

A useful way to study it: choose one support-document assistant, build a small baseline, and use the same evaluation questions as you improve it. That makes the tradeoffs visible.

Save the notebook and try one chapter in a real project. Which topic should I explain next?

items.title: AI engineering from scratch
items.caption:
A large AI curriculum is easier to use when you choose a destination first.

AI Engineering from Scratch, maintained by Rohit Ghumare and contributors, currently lists 542 lessons across 20 phases. Its four core paths connect AI applications, software foundations, agent-assisted engineering and product delivery.

Choose one path, build one working artifact, and keep the test results. Progress becomes easier to assess when you can show what works and where it fails.

The course is open source under MIT. Counts checked on 28 October 2026. Explore the original project: https://aiengineeringfromscratch.com/

items.title: Track website changes with Firecrawl
items.caption:
An agent monitoring a web page should be able to tell you what changed.

Firecrawl’s change tracking compares a tracked scrape with its previous snapshot. You can request a Git-style line diff or a structured field comparison, then decide which changes matter to your workflow.

That is useful for documentation, release notes and other sources that evolve. The first scrape establishes a baseline; a later scrape can return the difference. Scheduling those checks is a separate part of the system.

The prices in this graphic are illustrative. Documentation: https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/change-tracking

items.title: The new-model hype cycle
items.caption:
A new model drops. We declare a new era. Then the next model drops.

The excitement is understandable. But the useful question stays the same: does this model perform better on the work you actually need done?

Keep a small set of real tasks. Compare quality, latency, cost and the failures you can tolerate. Let that evidence decide what goes into your workflow.

items.title: 16 AI concepts worth understanding
items.caption:
Sixteen AI concepts become much easier to remember when you can see how they connect.

The first row covers model foundations. The next adds knowledge and context. Training and evaluation shape behavior, while agents and production controls turn model output into useful actions.

These are building blocks, not a requirement to put all sixteen into every product. Start with the task, identify what is missing, and test the next addition.
